title: .Value (ValueBase objects)
summary: The stored data inside value objects — IntValue, BoolValue, StringValue, NumberValue, ObjectValue, etc. The VALUE lives in .Value; the object itself is a container. Forgetting .Value is a classic bug.

properties.name: Value
properties.description: IntValue: number (integer), NumberValue: number (float), BoolValue: boolean, StringValue: string, ObjectValue: Instance reference, Color3Value: Color3, CFrameValue, Vector3Value…

events.name: Changed
events.description: Fires when Value changes — note it passes the NEW VALUE, not a property name (unlike Instance.Changed).

explanation.whatItIs: Value objects are boxes with one slot. The slot is .Value. You almost never want the box itself — you want what's in the slot.
explanation.whyItExists: The instance hierarchy can only hold instances; value objects wrap plain data so it can be parented, replicated, and watched with events.
whenToUse: Replicated simple state with change events
ObjectValue for references (e.g., 'this zone belongs to that Team')
whenNotToUse: As your primary data model — tables in code/DataStores are usually better
Where attributes suffice — attributes cover most simple per-instance data without extra objects
explanation.mentalModel:
```text
Coins (IntValue)
   └─ .Value = 50     ← the actual data

coins.Value + 1       ✔
coins + 1             ✘ (you're adding an instance!)
```
tips: leaderstats uses these: the leaderboard displays each child's .Value automatically
Changed on value objects passes the new value — different signature from Instance.Changed
Attributes often replace value objects for new projects
commonMistakes: Using the object instead of .Value: `label.Text = coins` instead of coins.Value
Comparing the object to a number: `if coins == 50` is always false
Creating value objects for data that could be an attribute

examples.title: leaderstats IntValue in action
examples.code:
local stats = Instance.new("Folder")
stats.Name = "leaderstats"

local coins = Instance.new("IntValue")
coins.Name = "Coins"
coins.Value = 0
coins.Parent = stats
stats.Parent = player

-- Reading/writing always through .Value:
coins.Value += 10
print(coins.Value)   --> 10

coins.Changed:Connect(function(newValue)
    print("Coins is now", newValue)   -- passes the VALUE
end)
